slot.brief: Figure shows d-orbital shapes; ask which orbital is shown (dx²−y² etc.) or which orbitals point along axes.

stem: The boundary surface diagram of a 3d orbital is shown in the figure. Identify the orbital.
working: The figure shows four lobes directed along the x and y axes only, with no torus and no lobes along z. This matches the d(x^2 - y^2) orbital. d(xy) has lobes between the x and y axes; d(yz) has lobes between y and z; d(xz) has lobes between x and z.
solution: The $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital has four lobes directed along the $x$- and $y$-axes. The figure shows this orientation, so the orbital is $d_{x^2-y^2}$.

draft.stem: The boundary surface diagram of a 3d orbital is shown in the figure. Identify the orbital.

figure.description: Draw three mutually perpendicular axes labelled x, y and z with the origin at the centre. Draw four identical elongated lobes in one plane: one lobe extending from the origin along the positive x-axis, one along the negative x-axis, one along the positive y-axis, and one along the negative y-axis. The lobes should meet at the origin and have their long axes along the x and y directions. No lobes or torus should be drawn along the z-axis.

draft.working: The figure shows four lobes directed along the x and y axes only, with no torus and no lobes along z. This matches the d(x^2 - y^2) orbital. d(xy) has lobes between the x and y axes; d(yz) has lobes between y and z; d(xz) has lobes between x and z.
draft.distractor_notes: B: confuses lobes between the x and y axes with axial lobes. C: confuses lobes between the y and z axes with the d(yz) orbital. D: confuses lobes between the x and z axes with the d(xz) orbital.
